newsitem.title: SPAIN: No need to quiz Gonzalez--for now.
newsitem.headline: No need to quiz Gonzalez--for now.

text.p: Spain's state prosecutors told the Supreme Court on Monday there are no grounds to question former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez about a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels -- but that this could yet change.

Gonzalez, who lost elections in March after 13 years in power, denies charges by former security chiefs and disgruntled fellow Socialists that he knew of the 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murders by members of the security forces and hired gunmen.

The Supreme Court's second chamber, which deals with cases involving members of parliament like Gonzalez, was due to decide later on Monday or on Tuesday whether to call him in a ruling with huge implications for his political future.
Prosecutor Jose Maria Luzon's advice against questioning the former prime minister was important but not binding on the court -- and his boss said it may yet change if new evidence surfaces.

"This decision has no bearing on others which, should there be new elements to take into account, could be taken while the investigation proceeds," Attorney-General Juan Ortiz Urculo said in a statement after Luzon's appearance at the Supreme Court.
The proceedings adjourned for lunch, Spanish style, from 2.30 p.m. to 5 p.m. (1600 GMT).
Gonzalez himself was not in court on Monday but called a news conference about the refugee crisis in Central Africa and refused to answer any questions about the top tribunal's impending ruling.
"How am I waiting for it? This is how I'm waiting," he told reporters who asked about the proceedings.

Technically, the 10 judges were deciding on an appeal about whether the Socialist leader should be questioned in the chief case in the covert anti-guerrilla campaign -- the kidnapping in December 1983 of Basque businessman Segundo Marey.
One of the judges, investigating justice Eduardo Moner, has already ruled that there is insufficient evidence to summon him.
The second chamber's ruling will be on an appeal against that decision, lodged by relatives of the victims.

The only new accusations against Gonzalez since Moner's decision in April have come from Luis Roldan, a former Socialist head of the paramilitary Civil Guard who is himself accused of fraud and embezzlement while in office.
Roldan has testified that the anti-ETA operations were official government policy and that Gonzalez was fully involved.

Gonzalez's first interior minister, Jose Barrionuevo, is already on trial at the Supreme Court on charges of masterminding and funding the shadowy death squads known as the GAL (the Spanish initials for Anti-terrorist Liberation Groups).
A senior Civil Guard general who commanded the force's main base in the Basque country is also on trial.

The conservative government of Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, winner of the March election, has accused Gonzalez of having waged "bodeguilla terrorism" -- a reference to a wine-cellar in his official residence where he entertained friends and hatched strategies with his closest aides.
